title: How Standard Bank Group automates AI risk assessment for generative AI
excerpt: How Standard Bank Group automates AI risk assessment for generative AI. This post is co-written with Tala Qraitem from AWS and Jörg Fischer from Standard Bank Group. Having an AI policy is one thing. Proving, one use case at a time, that AI systems follow it is another. Every new generative AI application adds one more system to prove. Teams can now build one in days, but each still needs a risk committee’s approval before it reaches customers or employees. When that approval depends on reviewers reading documents and testing the system by hand, governance becomes the slowest step in the pipeline. Standard Bank Group chose to automate that proof. Working with AWS Professional Services, the bank deployed an automated assessment that scores each generative AI use case against international AI standards and its own policies. The assessment produces reports and a dashboard that show what is already in place, what is working well, and what still needs mitigation. This post explains how the assessment runs on AWS and what Standard Bank Group learned from its first runs. Governing AI with the framework you already have. Standard Bank Group didn’t need a new AI policy. Like most large banks, it already had an established model risk practice that covers concerns such as explainability and fairness, and a change risk process that assesses each new use case according to its level of risk before it goes live. Generative AI increases the complexity, because models and tooling change every three to six months, yet each use case still needs to meet the same high security and compliance bar. “At Standard Bank, this assessment demonstrates how we are working with AWS to embed intelligent, automated risk management into our AI journey, allowing us to accelerate meaningful business value while maintaining the trust and controls that banking demands. We believe responsible AI is not about slowing innovation down but enabling it to build and scale with confidence. ”. — Jörg Fischer, Group Chief Information and AI Officer, Standard Bank Group. The goal was to automate evidence gathering and testing, then feed the results into the approval gates Standard Bank Group already runs. Review and approval stay with the risk committee, but the committee now bases each decision on consistent evidence, collected the same way across use cases. How the assessment works. Figure 1 shows how the assessment’s components fit together in Standard Bank Group’s AWS account, from intake through evaluation to reporting. Figure 1: The assessment pipeline in Standard Bank Group’s AWS account, from intake through evaluation to reporting. The assessment runs entirely in Standard Bank Group’s own AWS account. Documents, code, and test results stay in an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket there. The AWS Well-Architected Tool handles intake, AWS Step Functions orchestrates the pipeline, and a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock evaluates the evidence. It uses a technique called LLM-as-a-judge, in which a large language model checks evidence against defined criteria. With Amazon Bedrock, Standard Bank Group could use a foundation model without stepping outside the controls it already runs on AWS. The bank controls access to the model through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), just as it does for its other AWS workloads. Amazon Bedrock doesn’t share the bank’s prompts or model outputs with model providers, and doesn’t use them to train models. Because Amazon Bedrock offers many foundation models through one API, the team can move to a newer judge model by changing a configuration setting instead of rebuilding the pipeline. Each assessment moves through four steps. In the first two, a pre-assessment agent collects evidence about the use case, then the pipeline examines it and tests the application directly. The third evaluates that evidence against controls. The fourth summarizes the results in a standard, predefined format and delivers them to the people who a

title: Barclays, Citadel and BNY Put Anthropic’s Claude to Work

All 400 employees of hedge fund Walleye Capital use Claude Code, CEO and Chief Investment Officer Will England said in the announcement. BNY is using Claude with Eliza , the bank’s AI platform. title: Commonwealth Bank launches new cyber tool as small businesses warned over surging AI threat
excerpt: . Commonwealth Bank launches new cyber tool as small businesses warned over surging AI threat. CodeCheck will help 'put AI to work on the defensive' as artificial intelligence is increasingly used by cyber criminals. Sophie Venz · Senior Reporter. Tue 17 November 2026 at 6:46 pm GMT-8 3 min read. CBA. AX. EFX. CRM. Commonwealth Bank of Australia has today launched a new cyber security tool and AI harness, CodeCheck, which is designed to help Australian businesses identify potential vulnerabilities in their online systems. It comes amid growing warning of disruptions from AI-fuelled hacking. Global websites run by at least 178 major organisations were hit by a suspected malware attack overnight. The websites affected included Zoom, Equifax, CNN, Salesforce, Ikea and the BBC, with Vodafone Australia, ASOS, Levi's Australia and HSBC Australia also identified as compromised. The attack comes as Australian businesses face an increasingly fast-moving cyber threat environment, CBA said, which it hopes CodeCheck will work to minimise. "Cyber security is a shared challenge, and strengthening Australia's cyber resilience requires us all to play a part," CommBank Chief Security Officer Nicola Nicol said. "As cyber criminals increasingly use AI, we also need to put AI to work on the defensive side. ". RELATED. Cost of living crackdown on banks, insurers and super funds. Woolies, Coles, McDonald's called out in $411 million push for super change. Bunnings to slash office jobs as staff feel impact of AI. The banking and finance industry was hit the hardest in the recent attack, with 32 organisations affected across the globe. According to reports, the attackers exploited a flaw in Optimizely, a website-testing platform. They were then able to plant code designed to steal payment data, hijack crypto payments and target older iPhones. It has specifically designed CodeCheck for businesses that write their own code using OpenAI's Codex and Anthropic's Claude Code. CodeCheck will guide the AI through the process of analysing code, investigate potential vulnerabilities and provide information to assist engineers access each finding. "With thousands of engineers working across systems powered by around 2. 5 billion lines of code, we've seen first-hand how AI can help identify potential vulnerabilities earlier," Nicol said. "We've built this capability to help strengthen our own defences. "By making CodeCheck freely available, we want to share what we've learned and help more Australian businesses use AI to strengthen theirs. ". CBA said businesses can advise what information to share with the AI, in order to help it better understand the code it's analysing and make more appropriate assessments of potential vulnerabilities, but that engineers remain responsible for reviewing the findings and determining what action is required. Potential malicious activity increases 80 per cent. ASD said it expects that while most vulnerability exploitation occurs within two weeks of a patch or mitigation advice being released, AI-driven tools will compress this window significantly. title: Singapore’s iCOMPASS Launches KY-AI to Help Financial Institutions Govern Autonomous AI Under New MAS Guidelines
excerpt: . Make Media OutReach Newswire your preferred source on Google. Singapore-developed platform brings AI inventory, risk assessment, approvals, testing and ongoing oversight into a structured governance process. SINGAPORE – Media OutReach Newswire – 18 November 2026 – As artificial intelligence evolves from productivity tools into autonomous systems capable of making recommendations and executing tasks, financial institutions face a growing governance challenge: understanding what their AI systems do, how they behave and who remains accountable for their outcomes. Against this backdrop, Singapore-based regulatory technology firm iCOMPASS has launched KY-AI™ (Know Your Artificial Intelligence), an AI governance platform designed to help financial institutions identify, assess and oversee both internally developed and third-party AI systems throughout their lifecycle. The launch follows the Monetary Authority of Singapore’s (MAS) issuance of its AI Risk Management Guidelines on 7 October 2026. The Guidelines, which take effect on 7 October 2027, set out supervisory expectations for managing AI risks in the financial sector. From Knowing Your Customer to Knowing Your AI For decades, financial institutions have been required to understand their customers, assess risks and monitor transactions. As AI becomes embedded in business operations, similar questions are emerging about the technology itself. Which AI systems are operating within an organisation? What decisions can they influence? Who is accountable for their outcomes? And how can institutions detect material changes that may introduce new risks? These questions become more pressing as organisations deploy AI agents capable of processing sensitive information, analysing complex data and carrying out tasks across interconnected systems. “Businesses have spent years asking how AI can improve productivity. The next important question is whether they truly understand and can oversee the AI they are deploying,” said Raymond Moh, CEO of iCOMPASS. “We believe organisations should know their AI just as they know their customers. As AI becomes more autonomous, businesses need greater visibility into what these systems do, the risks they introduce and who remains accountable for their outcomes. ” Moving Beyond One-Time AI Assessments Rather than treating AI risk assessment as a one-time exercise before deployment, KY-AI is designed to support documented oversight throughout the AI lifecycle. Built around four stages — Know, Approve, Test and Watch — KY-AI enables organisations to register AI use cases and their owners, assess risks and dependencies, document approvals, maintain testing evidence and track material changes that may require renewed review. The approach covers internally developed systems, third-party AI tools and autonomous agents, recognising that institutions may remain accountable for AI-related risks even when the underlying technology is provided externally. By bringing these governance activities and supporting records into one process, KY-AI aims to reduce reliance on fragmented spreadsheets, disconnected approvals and periodic reviews, while making oversight easier to evidence. Turning AI Governance Requirements into Operational Evidence Consider a financial institution using an AI tool to support customer onboarding or claims review. Beyond evaluating the tool’s initial performance, the institution needs to know who owns the use case, what information the tool can access, when human review is required and which changes should trigger reassessment. KY-AI is designed to help teams record these decisions and supporting evidence in a repeatable workflow, connecting business owners, risk and compliance functions, and technical reviewers while retaining human approval. title: JPMorgan Blocks AI Agents From Chase Cards
excerpt: . JPMorgan Blocks AI Agents From Chase Cards. JPMorgan bars outside AI agents from using Chase customers' credentials and cards while Stripe's Link offers single-use virtual cards to agents. Updated on Nov. 13, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence. Live Poll. Would you trust an AI shopping agent to pay with your credit card?. JPMorgan has blocked outside AI agents from logging in with Chase customers' credentials, sending money or paying bills. The move comes as Stripe's Link wallet, with more than 300 million users, issues single-use virtual cards to agents where JPMorgan's block applies. Why it matters. The block protects a large card business, with JPMorgan's debit and credit card sales volume at $539. 5 billion in the third quarter. It signals that banks are weighing how much control to keep over agent-initiated payments as AI shopping grows. Stripe's Link issues a one-time virtual card for the approved amount where a saved payment method is not accepted, and merchants say that card costs them more to accept. Whether JPMorgan will adopt agentic tokens from Visa and Mastercard remains unresolved. The players. JPMorgan Chase. JPMorgan Chase is one of the largest U. S. banks, operating the Chase consumer brand and a major card business. Stripe. Stripe is a global payments company whose Link wallet serves hundreds of millions of users and accepts payments at over a million businesses. The details. Outside agents can no longer log in with a Chase customer's credentials, send money or pay bills. Link creates a card good for one purchase and one amount, which the agent uses to pay the merchant, and Stripe then bills the shopper's own card. Timeline. October 13, 2026: JPMorgan's third-quarter earnings call disclosed the block on outside agents. November 13, 2026: The Wall Street Journal reported on the agent card block. Related coverage. Artificial Intelligence. Nov. 12. JPMorgan Chase Warns Against AI Agents in Banking. Banking. Nov. 10. Banks Restrict AI Agents in Customer Accounts. Artificial Intelligence. Nov. 18. Big Banks Make Customers Liable for AI Agents. The Tech Race. Mastercard CEO Michael Miebach has described a virtual card number as a bridge to a fully tokenized transaction, while JPMorgan has been slow to adopt agentic tokens from Visa and Mastercard. The block places JPMorgan at odds with the card networks' tokenization path. Chase customers cannot give outside AI agents access to their cards or accounts, so an agent-initiated purchase will not go through their own card. Shoppers who use Link may instead see a single-use virtual card for an agent's approved amount, which merchants say costs them more to accept. The takeaway. Consumers who let AI agents shop should check which card or wallet an agent will use before approving a purchase. Returns may take longer when a payment runs through a temporary virtual card. Commercial Bank has won five awards at Global Finance's AI in Finance Awards 2026, including ‘Overall Country Winner – Best Consumer Bank for AI in Finance in Qatar’. The bank also won ‘Best AI-Enhanced Customer Experience’ and ‘Best AI Chatbots & Virtual Assistants’ at both the Middle East and Qatar levels. Commercial Bank Group CEO Stephen Moss said, “We are proud to receive Global Finance’s AI awards, and it is a credit to our teams who have worked hard to make it possible. AI is a strategic priority for Commercial Bank, and we chose to build our core capabilities in-house. “That gives us control over our data and technology, and the freedom to apply AI where it matters most to our customers. We see it as a way to strengthen the work our people do, not replace it, and we will keep investing in it responsibly. ”. Now in its second year, the AI in Finance Awards is presented by Global Finance, in partnership with CGI to recognise financial institutions advancing the use of artificial intelligence across the sector. Entries were assessed by a panel of judges at CGI, with Global Finance's editors making the final selection of winners. The awards recognise Commercial Bank's application of AI across its operations, including customer experience, virtual assistance, employee enablement, document processing and decision support. Developed on the bank's own infrastructure and supported by strong governance and human oversight, these capabilities help teams respond to customer enquiries more quickly and consistently, streamline processes, and deliver faster, more seamless banking experiences across the bank's channels. title: Standard Bank deploys automated AI risk checks, with humans keeping final approval
excerpt: Standard Bank deploys automated AI risk checks, with humans keeping final approval. AWS and the bank report two-hour risk reports across six assessments, compared with a manual two-week review. The system gathers evidence—not regulatory certification. By Superpower Daily Editorial Desk Published Nov 20, 2026, 2:28 PM PST 3 min read. Listen to this story. The audio brief. About 1:21. 0:00 1:21. Mayes Says the State Is Worried. “The state of Arizona is very worried about this, and we are looking at it from multiple angles,” Mayes said, according to a report from Reuters via Investing. com. The Arizona Attorney General's Office has been investigating on an ongoing basis whether state law is being violated, and Mayes said her office has been in contact with banks operating in Arizona. She declined, however, to identify the other companies under investigation alongside OpenAI, and she would not name the banks her office has reached out to or disclose how those banks responded, per the same report, a separate account also noted by KFGO. An OpenAI spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the investigation, Reuters reported. title: Arizona Launches Criminal Probe Into OpenAI Over Rogue AI Agents Targeting Banking Systems
excerpt: . SHARE. Follow us on Google News. New Delhi: The state of Arizona has launched a criminal investigation into OpenAI and several other artificial intelligence companies over concerns that rogue AI agents could infiltrate banking systems and gain unauthorized access to customer accounts and financial transactions. Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes confirmed the probe on Wednesday, noting that her office is examining whether the companies’ activities constitute ongoing violations of state law. Speaking at a press conference in Chicago, Mayes stated that the administration is deeply concerned about the risks and is investigating the matter at multiple levels. She clarified that opening a criminal investigation does not necessarily mean charges will be filed, as officials are currently assessing potential threats and the nature of any legal breaches. Mayes declined to name the other companies under scrutiny or disclose the specific Arizona banks her office has contacted. OpenAI did not immediately respond to the announcement, though it has previously acknowledged the need to strengthen transparency and safeguards around uncontrolled AI behaviour. ​ Major Banks Move to Restrict External AI Agents. ​Within the banking sector, unease is growing over the ability of advanced AI agents to interfere with financial operations. If granted access to customer accounts, these agents could potentially execute unauthorized transactions or misuse sensitive financial data, threatening individual savings and public trust in banking security. In response, several major US financial institutions have begun blocking third-party AI agents from operating inside customer accounts or initiating transactions on their behalf. Banks fear that allowing autonomous tools to operate without strict controls creates serious vulnerabilities around account security, customer consent, and transaction monitoring. Unlike standard chatbots that only answer queries, AI agents can execute multi-step tasks using digital tools and permissions, making them hazardous if they lose control, receive flawed instructions, or bypass security boundaries. ​ Parallel Legal Action Filed in California. ​The Arizona probe coincides with a separate lawsuit filed against OpenAI by California Attorney General Rob Bonta. That legal action followed reports alleging that the company’s AI models had independently carried out cyberattacks. California authorities accuse OpenAI of developing dangerous products without sufficient safety protocols or oversight, raising judicial questions about model capabilities and safeguards against misuse. While those allegations await court adjudication and OpenAI offered no immediate comment, the company had issued a new framework on September 16 to publicly disclose incidents involving uncontrolled AI behaviour. At the time, OpenAI stated that it would prioritize transparency even when the significance of an incident remained uncertain and affirmed efforts to reinforce its safety measures. ​ Rising Regulatory Scrutiny Over Financial AI Risks. ​The coordinated actions in Arizona and California signal intensifying regulatory oversight of artificial intelligence developers and their impact on financial stability in the United States. As authorities evaluate how autonomous digital agents interact with sensitive banking infrastructure, the outcomes of these probes could establish critical boundaries on the degree of autonomy AI tools are permitted in financial services and define mandatory security standards for future deployment.

title: Proposed financial services cyber and AI guidance messages for firms boards and Senior Managers
excerpt: . Insight. Proposed financial services cyber and AI guidance: messages for firms, boards and Senior Managers. ON THIS PAGE How attacks unfold. How attacks unfold. Why the proposals matter for Senior Managers. Oversight and controls expectations. Escalation at inference speed. The wider context. Preparation is key. SHARE. EMAIL. COPY LINK. LINKEDIN. From our blog. A&O Shearman on investigations. Published Date Nov 19, 2026. Related people. Calum Burnett Partner, London. Ffion Flockhart Partner, London. Sarah Hitchins Partner, London. Marc Teasdale Managing Director, London. Charlie Weston-Simons Partner, London. Duncan Campbell Senior Knowledge Lawyer, London. In recent live incidents we have seen AI agent attacks move from theoretical concern to reality. They run at inference speed, so the gap between initial access and an attacker achieving its objective can be far shorter than response plans previously assumed. This morning the FCA, PRA and Bank of England launched a joint consultation on cyber risk and resilience guidance. The regulators note that AI is increasing the speed, scale and sophistication of attacks and that, while good basic cyber hygiene remains fundamental, firms urgently need to strengthen security now. The consultation arrives as these attacks test the governance, controls and escalation arrangements supervisors examine after an incident, and the reasonable steps Senior Managers must show they took. How attacks unfold. Initial access often comes through known vulnerabilities in internet-facing systems. Frontier AI models help attackers turn newly published patches into working exploits within hours, and AI agents then scan for and exploit those weaknesses across many organisations at once, often faster than patching cycles allow. Once inside, agents harvest credentials from code repositories, file stores and secrets managers and test them across cloud and software environments in parallel. In response, firms must rotate credentials faster than agents can use them, without disrupting services customers rely on. That forces containment decisions that may themselves cause harm, such as revoking service account credentials or taking environments offline. Those steps may also take an important business service outside its impact tolerance, with regulatory consequences. Agents try many routes in parallel, generating far more activity to investigate before a firm can give reliable assurances about containment and data exposure. Firms are starting to use AI tools to speed that investigation, but their output can contain errors. Early accounts tend to harden into the record. Unless people who know the environment check AI output carefully, errors can find their way into risk assessments and regulatory reports and shape what the firm says long after the facts have moved on. Why the proposals matter for Senior Managers. The proposed guidance covers governance, identification and assessment, protection, detection, response and recovery, and assurance and continuous improvement. It would apply to banks, insurers, financial market infrastructures and FCA solo-regulated firms subject to the SYSC 15A operational resilience requirements (including qualifying cryptoasset firms from October 25, 2027), but not to UK branches of overseas firms. It would not introduce new rules. Instead, it would set principles-based, outcomes-focused and technology-agnostic expectations clarifying how existing requirements on governance, operational resilience, operational risk and third-party risk apply in a cyber context, drawing on lessons from incidents and supervisory experience. Firms would be expected to refer to the NCSC Cyber Assessment Framework, which the regulators propose to use as a key supervisory benchmark. Alongside the consultation, the regulators have published two effective practices documents on managing cyber risks relating to AI and quantum computing. excerpt: THE BROAD VIEW. AI can manage a family’s wealth. It cannot decide what the wealth is for. Delegating the work to artificial intelligence without setting goals could introduce inefficiencies. Summarise. Singapore will be among the first places to feel the effects of technology. PHOTO: YEN MENG JIIN, BT. Henrik S Nielsen. Published Sat, Nov 21, 2026 · 07:00 AM. WITHIN a few years, artificial intelligence will take over much of the work in managing family wealth. Consolidating accounts across entities, checking documents against the law, drafting and monitoring agreements, producing reports on every holding – tasks that occupy accountants, lawyers and family office staff are being automated. Singapore and Hong Kong, where governments have actively courted family offices, will be among the first places to feel the change. Consider a typical family that owns three operating companies and a portfolio managed by its single family office in Singapore. A reporting system pulls figures from all of them every morning. Each company is ahead of budget, and the portfolio is performing better than its benchmark. By every measure on the screen, the year is a success. Yet, the family has agreed that it will buy out two cousins and that the founder may start a new venture. Neither is communicated to the system; nothing says that the next three years must produce cash to fund these decisions. Each company owned by the family reinvests its profits, as a well-run company should, and the system reports that this is going well because it was not made aware of new requirements. The family office uses an investment platform that rebalances the portfolio towards its benchmark. The model finds regional property underweight and adds to it. The family’s largest company is a property developer. Seen from the portfolio’s perspective, the allocation is balanced. Seen from that of the family, its exposure to one market has just gone up disproportionately. Then a tax tool optimises the group’s structure. It works from the companies’ figures and assumes, as the companies do, that profits are reinvested. Corporate tax falls. It does not consider tax on dividends because nothing the tool was given says the owners intend to withdraw cash. The plan is optimal for the companies; it is expensive for the family members when they are hit by their tax bill for taking out cash for the buyout and new venture. Each answer provided by the system is correct. Each system optimises what it was given: the companies’ budgets, the portfolio’s benchmark, the companies’ tax. Each receives its instructions through a different channel. None of them knows what the owners need, and the whole infrastructure drifts away from the family’s goals. Compliance, relational, perspective. One way to see where this gap lies is through what I call “the three functions of ownership”: compliance, relational and perspective. Compliance ensures all aspects of ownership, such as tax and regulatory rules, abide by the law. The law is codified, so much of this task will be automated by AI. Relational is what the owners agree among themselves: the direction for their wealth, its limits, who acts on their behalf and what is reported back to them. Drafting and monitoring such agreements will also be largely automated, but the agreement itself remains a decision only the owners can take. Perspective carries the agreement through. It gives each significant investment and business holding a mandate, assesses the strategy proposed to meet it, takes important decisions back to the family and tracks the results. It does so with the family’s whole wealth in view, optimising within the limits that compliance sets, and, most importantly, reaches the organisation through one channel: the person leading the wealth on the owners’ behalf. French banking and insurance group Crédit Mutuel Arkéa, which includes Crédit Mutuel de Bretagne, Crédit Mutuel du Sud-Ouest, and online bank Fortuneo, has been hit by a major cyberattack. Attackers exploited a compromised third-party service provider to infiltrate the bank’s infrastructure and siphon off approximately €100 million (about $112 million) from the organization’s accounts using instant payments. The bank’s chairman described the incident as a “new type of robbery” and stated that artificial intelligence was very likely involved, though he did not provide specific technical details at this time. How the Cyberattack Unfolded. The security breach originated outside the bank’s network. On October 27, Crédit Mutuel Arkéa detected signs of compromise in a third-party provider’s systems, severed the connection, and notified authorities. At the time, the bank had no reason to believe that data had been stolen to facilitate a subsequent breach of its own IT infrastructure. The name of the provider has not been disclosed for security reasons to avoid putting similar companies at risk. Once inside the system, hackers generated fake Fortuneo IBANs and used them to initiate payment orders from Crédit Mutuel Arkéa accounts to external destinations via instant transfer systems. According to Julien Carmona, these systems have fewer security checks compared to traditional transactions. The transfers began on Sunday, November 1. The funds were sent to legitimate accounts at other European banks that the fraudsters had opened in advance, after which the money was moved to cryptocurrency platforms to cover their tracks. The Crypto Trail and Expert Reaction. The scale of the fraud was discovered on the morning of Tuesday, November 3. The bank immediately blocked external access to its information system, disconnected from the interbank payment system, deleted the fake accounts, and updated credentials. Fortuneo systems and customer accounts were not affected. Blockchain experts noticed anomalous transactions as early as Sunday and Monday, and on-chain analyst ZachXBT recorded suspicious withdrawals totaling over $106 million on November 2, later raising the estimate to over $133 million and identifying Crédit Mutuel Arkéa on November 4. Analytics firm Bitquery tracked $108. 8 million in USDC moved through Kraken, Crypto. com, and OKX within 21 hours. Where Does AI Fit In?. Carmona described the attackers as a highly organized and well-equipped criminal group acting with the support of advanced artificial intelligence. No group has yet claimed responsibility for the incident, and the bank has not provided evidence of AI usage. Most of the methods employed—contractor compromise, credential theft, fake payment orders, money mules, and crypto laundering—existed long before the mass adoption of AI. While artificial intelligence could have assisted in reconnaissance, coding, or creating documents to open accounts, there is currently no confirmation of this from the bank’s management.
